Here is one of the map details I love following: a neighbourhood can cross ward lines. These wards overlap this neighbourhood on the City map. That tells us about boundaries, not how many residents live in each ward or whether a whole neighbourhood belongs to each one.

I include 30 whole City neighbourhoods with most of their land area in Scarborough. The City does not assign them to a Scarborough district in this dataset. DineSafe places follow a separate rule: they must lie within the six Scarborough wards.
Keep this patch of Scarborough in view: its neighbourhood page brings the map, dated records and boundary sources together. Pick a familiar place and follow its paper trail.
There is another set of boundaries to explore: provincial and federal ridings. They differ from City wards and neighbourhoods, so use your address to find the right MPP or MP.
There is no ward crime total here. TPS reports whole-neighbourhood quarterly summaries; dividing those up between wards would give a misleading number.
The quarterly TPS neighbourhood summaries are not ready to publish here. I do not show incident locations or current crime counts.

Planning applications and issued permits tell you different things. I have not finished checking these sources for Scarb.TO, so I am not showing them or making claims about construction. You can still look up applications with the City.

Scarborough has a lot of stories hiding in its data.

Scarborough's maps and public records give me plenty to get curious about. I've brought the places, inspection results and neighbourhood boundaries together here, with their dates and sources. Pick a thread. Let's see where it leads.

Here's a favourite Scarborough map quirk: City wards and neighbourhoods don't always line up. Try either boundary to narrow the food inspection map and list. Beach samples and police division totals use different areas.

Now this is a patch of Scarborough worth getting to know. I've put the food inspection records and City neighbourhood boundaries for {{NAME}} side by side. Start with a familiar place, then follow the source links. There's often another detail worth checking.

Pick a neighbourhood and follow its map. This directory has {{COUNT}} pages using names from the City of Toronto neighbourhood registry. This is Scarb.TO's retained map selection, not an official City membership list or a claim about current inspection conditions.
Let's turn local records into a neighbourhood update.

There's a lot tucked away in Scarborough's public records. Choose your patch and I'll bring the dated, source-linked findings together for print or your website. The evidence stays attached; you decide what to share.

A little map nerdiness before we begin: City neighbourhoods don't always stay inside Scarborough's six ward boundaries. For DineSafe, I count only records inside those wards, even if a selected neighbourhood carries on beyond them. These are editorial selections, not claimed newspaper or association territories.

Now for one of my favourite parts: where did this edition's information actually come from? Here's the saved source release, its dates and what those records can tell us. This page doesn't publicly store a publisher's own wording; import the finalised receipt to inspect the exact edition.
Here's what the records turned up for this area. I keep the source dates and links close by, because the trail behind a finding can be just as interesting as the finding itself.
The week's food inspection paper trail.
